reason: The tablet's sponsor app obstructs the request form, but it is not yet clear how to remove or replace it.
expectation: The compatibility list should show how to begin making the tablet suitable for voluntary requests.

alternatives.reason: The screwdriver might open the tablet, but the visible problem is an app rather than a confirmed hardware fault.

effect: The listening app is removed and the microphone physically disconnected; the tablet is ready for further request-desk work.
reaction: The physical disconnection makes the privacy change reassuringly concrete.
reason: A large request button is an obvious way to make the form deliberately accessible.
expectation: The button will give people a deliberate way to start a request.

effect: The button has no available combination yet, so another part of the request desk likely needs attention first.
reaction: I was premature in assuming the button could be fitted immediately.
reason: Checking the modified tablet should reveal the next available part of the setup.
expectation: The tablet's compatibility list will show how to continue preparing the request desk.

effect: The tablet now uses the local controller and has its outside network route blocked.
reaction: The local-only default makes the privacy protection more concrete.
reason: The request button may now be usable with the locally connected tablet; I am retrying it because the setup has changed.
expectation: The button will give people a deliberate way to start a request.

effect: The button now sends a written request only when pressed.

reason: The folded hood should give people more privacy while they write on the tablet.

effect: The hood shields the request form from the queue; the desk still needs any remaining components.
reaction: A simple cardboard shield is a satisfying privacy measure.
reason: The old receipt printer may give requesters a record of what they submitted.
expectation: The printer will add a printed receipt to the request desk.

effect: The printer now works through the local controller, producing receipts while keeping return details off the shared queue.
reaction: I was wrong about connecting it directly to the tablet, but the privacy controls are useful.
reason: The local queue printer and shielded request tablet appear to be the prepared parts of the request desk.
expectation: Combining them will complete a request desk with private submission and receipts.

effect: The tablet and printer now form a private request desk, though the goal has not yet been reported complete.
reaction: The pencil and paper option is a welcome alternative to speaking to a machine.
reason: Moth is the remaining obvious component to connect with the completed desk, though its exact role is unclear.

choice.combine: Moth with source display and correction controls

expectation: Moth may help handle requests from the desk while preserving the user's choice and access to corrections.

alternatives.reason: I could check its available partners first, but Moth appears to be the remaining relevant item.

effect: Moth adds optional rewriting with a preview, and the request desk goal is complete.
reaction: Sal keeping her original wording makes the choice feel tangible.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting Moth to the desk was most worthwhile: help is optional, its wording is shown before sending, and Sal can keep her own words.

leastWorthwhile.text: Retrying the button after discovering the tablet needed a local connection was a little repetitive, though the first failed attempt clarified the sequence.

surprise.text: The printer connected to the controller rather than directly to the tablet; the compatibility feedback performed that connection automatically.

arbitrary.text: The button's initial unavailability felt somewhat arbitrary until the tablet was connected locally; the result did not explain why that order was required.

continue.text: Yes. The concrete privacy choices and optional assistance made this chapter engaging, and I would be curious to see how the neighborhood uses the desk.
